description: The context as a step: Claude Haiku 5.5 answers from each context of the baseline's ranking, the named cards alone and then also their refs

metrics.name: Valid answers
metrics.what: Out of the questions, the share that got an answer in the expected format.
metrics.how: A reply is an answer when it holds a text, the ids it cites and whether the question can be answered, and nothing else. A reply that is not gets one more try. A question counts when one of its two tries is an answer. Then take the average over all the questions.
metrics.represents: Whether the player gets an answer at all. A question with no answer also gets 0 on answered or correct refusals, and on citation recall.

metrics.name: Answered
metrics.what: Out of the questions that have an answer, the share the Arbiter answers instead of refusing.
metrics.how: An answer refuses when it says the question can't be answered ("answerable" is false). Count 1 for an answer that does not refuse, 0 for one that does or for no answer. Questions that have no answer to give are left out. Then take the average over the questions.
metrics.represents: How rarely the Arbiter refuses by mistake: 100% means it never does. It says nothing of whether the answer is right, nor of the questions it should refuse: read it with correct refusals.

metrics.name: Correct refusals
metrics.what: Out of the questions that have no answer, the share the Arbiter refuses.
metrics.how: Count 1 for an answer that says the question can't be answered ("answerable" is false), 0 for one that answers it or for no answer. Only the questions that have no answer to give are scored. Then take the average over them.
metrics.represents: How rarely the Arbiter invents an answer: an answer to a question that has none can only be made up. Read it with answered, which a model that always refuses would fail.

metrics.name: Citation recall
metrics.what: Out of the rules and cards an answer must cite, the share it cites.
metrics.how: The answer key lists what a correct answer cites. Count how many of them the answer cites, then divide by how many there are: 2 out of 7 gives 29%. A question with no answer gets 0. Questions that have no answer to give are left out. Then take the average over the questions.
metrics.represents: Whether an answer cites everything it relies on. It does not look at what else the answer cites: read it with citation precision.

metrics.name: Citation precision
metrics.what: Out of the ids an answer cites that are right or wrong, the share that are right.
metrics.how: A cited id is right when the answer key lists it. Two kinds are tolerated, and neither counted right nor wrong: a rule an event of the scenario carries without being a key event (a spell going to the graveyard), and a card the question names. Any other id is wrong. Divide the right ones by the right and the wrong ones: 1 right and 1 wrong gives 50%. Answers that cite only tolerated ids or nothing, and questions that have no answer to give, are left out. Then take the average over the questions.
metrics.represents: Whether an answer cites only what it should. Citing the cards the question names neither helps nor hurts. It does not look at what the answer leaves out: read it with citation recall.

metrics.name: Step order
metrics.what: Whether an answer cites the rules of a scenario in the order they apply.
metrics.how: A scenario's key events happen one after the other, each with its rules. Take every pair of cited rules from two different events, then count the pairs cited in the order the events happen: 5 out of 6 gives 83%. Only scenarios are scored, when the answer cites rules of at least two of their events. Then take the average over the questions.
metrics.represents: Whether an answer gives a chain of effects in the right order. One rule out of place costs a few pairs, not the whole score.

metrics.name: Valid answers: questions
metrics.what: How many questions Valid answers scored.
metrics.how: The questions Valid answers applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Valid answers. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Answered: questions
metrics.how: The questions Answered applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Answered. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Correct refusals: questions
metrics.what: How many questions Correct refusals scored.
metrics.how: The questions Correct refusals applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Correct refusals. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Citation recall: questions
metrics.what: How many questions Citation recall scored.
metrics.how: The questions Citation recall applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Citation recall. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Citation precision: questions
metrics.what: How many questions Citation precision scored.
metrics.how: The questions Citation precision applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Citation precision. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Step order: questions
metrics.what: How many questions Step order scored.
metrics.how: The questions Step order applies to, as its own description says.
metrics.represents: How much to trust Step order. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Questions
metrics.how: Every question of the split, or of one category, those that have no answer to give included.
metrics.represents: How much to trust a score. The fewer the questions, the more a single question moves it.

metrics.name: Input tokens
metrics.what: How many tokens the model reads for a question, on average.
metrics.how: Add up the input tokens of every try at a question, then take the average over all the questions.
metrics.represents: Most of it is the context: it grows with every chunk the prompt holds.

metrics.name: Output tokens
metrics.what: How many tokens the model writes for a question, on average, its thinking included.
metrics.how: Add up the output tokens of every try at a question, then take the average over all the questions.
metrics.represents: How much the model writes and thinks, which the latency and the cost follow.

metrics.name: Cost
metrics.what: What a question costs, on average, in US dollars.
metrics.how: For each question, the tokens of every try at the model's list price per million tokens, input and output apart. Then take the average over all the questions.
metrics.represents: What an answer costs to serve. Lower is better.

metrics.name: Latency p50
metrics.what: How long a typical answer takes.
metrics.how: For each question, add up the time of every try. The p50 is the time that half of the questions don't go over.
metrics.represents: How long a player waits for the answer once the context is chosen, as the model's API took when the answer was first written. Lower is better.

metrics.name: Latency p95
metrics.what: How long the slowest answers take.
metrics.how: For each question, add up the time of every try. The p95 is the time that 95% of the questions don't go over.
metrics.represents: How long a player waits for the answer once the context is chosen, as the model's API took when the answer was first written. Lower is better.

answer.answer: Casting Roaring Pyre first gives all your units +3/+0 until end of turn, so Ash Warden gets +3 attack for the rest of the turn. Casting Tempest next destroys all units, so your Ash Warden is destroyed, and the +3/+0 bonus ends with it. Your opponent has no unit to lose, so Tempest only affects your side. The context does not say whether you can afford both spells (2 + 7 = 9 Shards in total).

Swell first gives all your units +1/+1 until they leave the board, so Ash Warden becomes 7 defense and Reefkeeper becomes 7 defense. Tempest then destroys all units, including both of yours, regardless of their defense. Nothing in the context protects them from destruction, so both leave the board and the +1/+1 is lost with them. Your opponent has no units, so nothing on their side is affected. The context does not give the rules for Shard totals or whether you can pay for Swell (2 Shards) and Tempest (7 Shards) in the same turn, so I can't say whether you can afford both.

Casting Roaring Pyre first gives all your units +3/+0 until end of turn, so Ashborn Drake gets +3 power for the rest of the turn. Casting Tempest next destroys all units, so Ashborn Drake is destroyed despite its 11 defense and the buff. Your opponent has no units, so Tempest destroys only your Drake. The two spells cost 2 and 7 Shards, 9 in total. The context does not say whether you have that many Shards. Nothing in the context protects Drake, so the Anchor rule does not stop its destruction.

Kindle resolves first: Ash Warden's Kindle (1 Shard) gives all your units +2/+0 until end of turn, so Ashborn Drake and Ash Warden both get the bonus. Then Tempest (7 Shards) resolves and destroys all units. Both your Ashborn Drake and Ash Warden are destroyed, and the +2/+0 bonus is lost with them. Your opponent has no units, so nothing of theirs is affected. The Kindle bonus does not protect either unit, because the context gives Tempest no exception and neither unit is protected.

Swell resolves first: for 2 Shards, all your units get +1/+1, so Ashborn Drake becomes 12 defense and Reefkeeper becomes 7 defense. Then Tempest (7 Shards) resolves and destroys all units. That includes both of your units, whatever their defense, so Ashborn Drake and Reefkeeper are both destroyed and the board has no units left. The +1/+1 from Swell is lost with them. Your opponent has no units, so nothing of theirs is affected. Nothing in the context protects your units from destruction, so Tempest's effect applies in full.

Tempest resolves first: it destroys all units, so Cinderling and Shoal Sprite both leave the board. Each one's Death ability then triggers and waits to resolve, as the triggered-ability rule says. Cinderling's Death deals 2 damage to its controller's opponent, which is you, so you go from 20 HP to 18 HP. Shoal Sprite's Death makes its controller's opponent draw 1 card, so your opponent draws 1 card. The order in which these two triggers resolve is set by rule 9.8, which is not in my context, so I cannot confirm which goes first. The result is the same either way unless a draw from an empty deck is involved, and I don't have information on either deck. I am also assuming that destruction counts as dying for Death abilities, which the context does not state.

Tempest resolves first and destroys both Cinderling and Shoal Sprite. Their Death abilities then trigger and wait. Since you cast Tempest, you are the active player, so your own triggers resolve first, but you have none. Your opponent's triggers resolve next, in board order: Cinderling's Death deals 2 damage to you, taking you from 2 HP to 0 HP. You lose, because a player wins when their opponent's HP drops to 0 or less. Shoal Sprite's Death, which draws your opponent 1 card, would come after Cinderling's, but the game is already decided. You are not at 0 HP at the same time as your opponent, so the game is not a draw.

Cinderfall resolves first: it deals 4 damage to each of your opponent's units. Cinderling (2 defense) and Shoal Sprite (2 defense) both take lethal damage and leave the board. Their Death abilities then trigger. Because you are the active player, the opponent's abilities resolve in arrival order, so Cinderling's Death resolves first: it deals 2 damage to its controller's opponent, which is you, taking you from 20 HP to 18 HP. Next, Shoal Sprite's Death resolves: its controller draws 1 card. Final result: you are at 18 HP, your opponent has no units on the board, and your opponent has drawn 1 card.

Cinderfall resolves first: it deals 4 damage to each of your opponent's units. Cinderling (2 defense) and Shoal Sprite (2 defense) both die. Their Death abilities then trigger and wait. Both belong to your opponent, who is not the active player, so they resolve in arrival order: Cinderling first. Cinderling's Death deals 2 damage to its controller's opponent, which is you. You go from 2 HP to 0, so you lose. Shoal Sprite's Death (draw 1 card) would resolve after that, but the game is already over. Your opponent stays at 20 HP, so this is not a draw.

Tempest resolves first and destroys all units, so your opponent's Shoal Sprite and Cinderling both leave the board at once. Their Death abilities then trigger and wait. Since you are the active player and have no units on the board, your opponent's triggers resolve next, in order of arrival. Shoal Sprite arrived first, so its Death resolves first: your opponent draws 1 card. Cinderling's Death resolves next: it deals 2 damage to its controller's opponent, which is you, so you go from 20 HP to 18 HP. Tempest itself deals no damage to players.

Tempest resolves first and destroys all units, including yours and your opponent's. Each unit's Death ability then triggers and waits. Both triggers belong to your opponent, so they resolve in the order the units arrived: Shoal Sprite first, so your opponent draws 1 card, then Cinderling, which deals 2 damage to its opponent, which is you. You are at 2 HP, so you drop to 0 and lose the game. If you control units with Death abilities, those trigger first because you are the active player, but the context does not show any, so this ruling assumes you have none.

Cinderfall deals 4 damage to each enemy unit. Shoal Sprite and Cinderling each have 2 defense, so both are destroyed. Cinderfall finishes resolving before their Death abilities trigger (9.11). Both Death abilities belong to your opponent, so they resolve in the order the units arrived: Shoal Sprite first, then Cinderling. Shoal Sprite's Death makes your opponent draw 1 card. Cinderling's Death deals 2 damage to its controller's opponent, which is you, so you go from 20 HP to 18 HP. Your opponent ends with 1 extra card and you end at 18 HP.

Cinderfall deals 4 damage to each of your opponent's units. Shoal Sprite (2 defense) and Cinderling (2 defense) both die. Cinderfall finishes resolving completely before their Death abilities resolve. Those abilities belong to your opponent, who is not the active player, so they resolve in arrival order: first Shoal Sprite's Death draws your opponent 1 card, then Cinderling's Death deals 2 damage to you, its controller's opponent. You go from 2 HP to 0 and lose; your opponent wins because they stay at 20 HP, so it is not a draw.

Binding Thread is a Neutral spell costing 1 Shard. When played, it links two units. The link lasts until the link breaks, which happens when either linked unit leaves the board. While linked, when one of them takes damage from an attack or a spell, the damage is shared: the unit hit takes half, rounded up, and the linked unit takes the rest. The transferred share is not shared again. For example, 3 damage to a linked unit means 2 to it and 1 to its partner. A unit can only have one link, and a unit that is already linked cannot be chosen for a new Link.

You do. During your opponent's turn, you are the non-active player, and you make the choices that rules or effects ask of you while they resolve. That includes deciding whether to intercept an attack that targets one of your units, and choosing an echo's new target (if it has a target) or which cards to discard when an effect asks for that.

Playing a card: first you pay its cost. Its cost is its printed cost (or the cost of its next Fracture step), plus every cost change from auras, and minus 2 if you overcharge it. If the total is below 0, it costs 0. Overcharging is optional: when you play a card with Overcharge you may choose to overcharge it, and it then costs 2 Shards less, never below 0. Overcharge only reduces the cost of playing the card, never the cost of an attack ability. Then the card is resolved: a unit or relic arrives on the board and its Arrival abilities trigger; a spell applies its effect, then goes to the graveyard. A Fracture card instead applies its next step, and after a step that is not the last one it returns to its owner's hand instead of going to the graveyard, unless the hand is full, in which case it goes to the graveyard and its progress is lost. A Fracture card with a sacrifice cost pays it at each step.

When a card is returned to hand, it loses all of its modifications and all of its damage (rule 6.7; rule 8.8 applies the same to units and relics returned by a Return to hand effect). It does not die, so nothing that triggers on dying happens. If your hand is full, the card goes to the graveyard instead, still without dying.

To sacrifice a unit means to destroy one of your own units, whether as a cost of a card or as an effect. The sacrificed unit dies. A sacrifice is never partial: you can only play a card or use an ability if you can make every sacrifice it asks for. If you have more units than the effect asks for, you choose which one is sacrificed. An anchored unit can be sacrificed; it counts as sacrificed and the sacrifice is still paid, but it stays on the board, so it frees no place.

While the unit is protected, nothing can make it leave the board: no destruction, no return to hand, no sacrifice, and no death at 0 defense. If an effect tries to make it leave, only that part of the effect is ignored, and the rest of the card still applies normally. If you sacrifice the anchored unit to pay a cost, the sacrifice still counts as paid, so the card's effect applies, but the unit stays on the board.

Yes. Once the protection is over, the unit can be destroyed, returned to hand or sacrificed normally again. Anchor protects a unit from its arrival until the start of its controller's next turn. While protected it can take damage and debuffs, but nothing can make it leave the board: no destruction, no return to hand, no sacrifice, and no death at 0 defense. If it drops to 0 defense while protected it is doomed, staying on the board and still able to intercept and attack; if its defense goes back above 0 it is no longer doomed. If the protection ends with its defense still at 0, it is destroyed at the end of that turn, unless a Turn end ability heals it first.

Reefkeeper's Spine Lash has no Echo, so nothing happens from it. Ash Warden's Cinder Bite has Echo 50, and the context suggests that if the unit dies, its Echo replays Cinder Bite for free, with a new target chosen by you: 4 damage halved to 2. Because your opponent has no unit, they can be targeted, so they would take 2 damage. The context does not say whether destruction counts as dying, though. Playing a card: first you pay its cost. Its cost is its printed cost (or the cost of its next Fracture step), plus every cost change from auras, and minus 2 if you overcharge it. If the total is below 0, it costs 0. Overcharging is optional: when you play a card with Overcharge you may choose to overcharge it, and it then costs 2 Shards less, never below 0. Overcharge only reduces the cost of playing the card, never the cost of an attack ability. Then the card is resolved: a unit or relic arrives on the board and its Arrival abilities trigger; a spell applies its effect, then goes to the graveyard. A Fracture card instead applies its next step, and after a step that is not the last one it returns to its owner's hand instead of going to the graveyard, unless the hand is full, in which case it goes to the graveyard and its progress is lost. A Fracture card with a sacrifice cost pays it at each step.

When a card is returned to hand, it loses all of its modifications and all of its damage (rule 6.7; rule 8.8 applies the same to units and relics returned by a Return to hand effect). It does not die, so nothing that triggers on dying happens. If your hand is full, the card goes to the graveyard instead, still without dying.

To sacrifice a unit means to destroy one of your own units, whether as a cost of a card or as an effect. The sacrificed unit dies. A sacrifice is never partial: you can only play a card or use an ability if you can make every sacrifice it asks for. If you have more units than the effect asks for, you choose which one is sacrificed. An anchored unit can be sacrificed; it counts as sacrificed and the sacrifice is still paid, but it stays on the board, so it frees no place.

While the unit is protected, nothing can make it leave the board: no destruction, no return to hand, no sacrifice, and no death at 0 defense. If an effect tries to make it leave, only that part of the effect is ignored, and the rest of the card still applies normally. If you sacrifice the anchored unit to pay a cost, the sacrifice still counts as paid, so the card's effect applies, but the unit stays on the board.

Yes. Once the protection is over, the unit can be destroyed, returned to hand or sacrificed normally again. Anchor protects a unit from its arrival until the start of its controller's next turn. While protected it can take damage and debuffs, but nothing can make it leave the board: no destruction, no return to hand, no sacrifice, and no death at 0 defense. If it drops to 0 defense while protected it is doomed, staying on the board and still able to intercept and attack; if its defense goes back above 0 it is no longer doomed. If the protection ends with its defense still at 0, it is destroyed at the end of that turn, unless a Turn end ability heals it first.
